cards.front: What is an enzyme's turnover number, kcat?
cards.back: How many substrate molecules one busy (substrate-holding) enzyme converts per second. Units: s⁻¹.
cards.quote: Only busy enzymes make product, and each works at its own fixed pace, its turnover number, kcat: how many substrate molecules one busy enzyme converts per second.

cards.front: In the simplest enzyme scheme, velocity is how fast one busy enzyme works times how much enzyme is busy: v = {{c1::kcat × [ES]}}.
cards.quote: An enzyme's velocity is how fast one busy enzyme works times how much of the enzyme is busy: in the simplest scheme, v = kcat × [ES].

cards.front: For a Michaelis–Menten enzyme, the busy fraction is [S]/(Km + [S]). What do saturation, Vmax and Km each mean in terms of that fraction?
cards.back: Saturation: the fraction climbing toward 1. Vmax: every enzyme busy. Km: the [S] at which half the enzyme is busy.
cards.quote: Saturation is that fraction climbing toward 1; Vmax is every enzyme busy; Km is the substrate concentration at which half the enzyme is busy.

cards.front: What single property of a reversible enzyme inhibitor decides how it changes the v versus [S] curve?
cards.back: Which pool of enzyme it pulls out of the working pool: free enzyme (E), busy enzyme (ES), or both.
cards.quote: An inhibitor pulls enzyme out of the working pool, and which pool it pulls from (free enzyme, busy enzyme, or both) decides how the curve changes.

cards.front: What does thermodynamics tell you about a reaction, and what does kinetics tell you?
cards.back: Thermodynamics: whether the reaction can happen (the destination). Kinetics: how fast it happens (the journey).
cards.quote: Thermodynamics tells you the destination: whether a reaction can happen. Kinetics tells you the journey: how fast.
cards.section: Measuring the reaction: the assay and V₀

cards.front: Before converting substrate to product, an enzyme binds it and forms a temporary {{c1::enzyme–substrate (ES) complex}}: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P.
cards.quote: An enzyme first has to grab its substrate and hold it, forming a temporary enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, before converting it to product:
cards.section: Measuring the reaction: the assay and V₀

cards.front: In an enzyme assay, why is velocity taken as the initial slope (V₀) of product versus time rather than a later slope?
cards.back: The product curve starts straight, then bends as substrate is depleted, product accumulates and interferes, and the enzyme loses activity. Only the first moments reflect the [S] you added.
cards.quote: Plot product against time and the line starts straight, then bends as substrate is depleted, product accumulates and interferes, and the enzyme loses activity.
cards.section: Measuring the reaction: the assay and V₀

cards.front: In the simple Michaelis–Menten scheme, name the one way into the ES state and the two ways out, with their rates.
cards.back: In: substrate binds empty enzyme, k₁[E][S]. Out without product: substrate falls off, k₋₁[ES]. Out with product: k₂[ES] (k₂ is kcat here).
cards.quote: In: substrate collides with an empty enzyme and sticks, at k₁[E][S].
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: Why does enzyme velocity level off as substrate concentration keeps rising?
cards.back: More substrate speeds the way into ES (binding) but not the ways out (falling off, turnover). Once nearly every enzyme is busy (saturated), no empty ones are left to fill.
cards.quote: Adding substrate speeds up the way in but does nothing to the ways out.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: What is the steady-state assumption at the centre of the Michaelis–Menten model?
cards.back: Soon after mixing (usually within milliseconds), enzymes become busy as fast as they stop being busy, so [ES] holds steady: k₁[E][S] = (k₋₁ + k₂)[ES].
cards.quote: Soon after mixing, usually within milliseconds, enzymes become busy as fast as they stop being busy, and the number of busy enzymes holds steady.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: In the steady-state derivation, the Michaelis constant collects the rate constants: Km = {{c1::(k₋₁ + k₂) / k₁}}.
cards.quote: Collect the rate constants into one number: [E][S] / [ES] = (k₋₁ + k₂) / k₁.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: The Michaelis–Menten equation: v = {{c1::Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])}}.
cards.back: A hyperbola rising toward Vmax but never reaching it.
cards.quote: So v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). That is the Michaelis–Menten equation
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: In the Michaelis–Menten model, Vmax equals what product of enzyme quantities?
cards.back: kcat × [E]ₜ: the speed with every enzyme molecule busy.
cards.quote: The left side becomes v; kcat[E]ₜ, the speed with every enzyme busy, is Vmax.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: The Michaelis–Menten curve has the same shape as which protein-binding curve, and what plays the role of Kd?
cards.back: Single-site binding, Y = L/(Kd + L). Km takes the place of Kd (but the two constants are not the same thing).
cards.quote: It has the shape of single-site binding in protein binding, Y = L/(Kd + L), with Km in place of Kd.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: Under what three conditions does the simple Michaelis–Menten equation apply?
cards.back: One substrate; far more substrate than enzyme (so free [S] is about the [S] added); velocity measured at the initial rate.
cards.quote: Its scope: one substrate, far more substrate than enzyme (so free [S] is about the [S] you added), measured at initial velocity.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: An enzyme has Vmax = 60 µmol/min and Km = 4 mM. Find v at [S] = 12 mM and at 24 mM. By what percentage did doubling [S] raise v?
cards.back: 12 mM: busy fraction 12/16 = 0.75, v = 45 µmol/min. 24 mM: 24/28 ≈ 0.86, v ≈ 51 µmol/min. About 14% faster.
cards.why: Only a quarter of the enzyme was empty at 12 mM, so doubling substrate had little left to fill: saturation.
cards.quote: At [S] = 12 mM the busy fraction is 12 / (4 + 12) = 0.75, so v = 0.75 × 60 = 45 µmol/min.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: For a Michaelis–Menten enzyme, what [S], as a multiple of Km, gives 95% of Vmax?
cards.back: 19 Km. A fraction f needs [S] = (f / (1 − f)) × Km = (0.95/0.05) × Km = 19 Km.
cards.quote: In general, a fraction f needs [S] = (f / (1 − f)) × Km, so 80% needs 4 Km.
cards.section: Building the curve: how much of the enzyme is busy

cards.front: Why is Km not a measure of an enzyme's binding affinity for substrate?
cards.back: Km = Kd + k₂/k₁. Turnover is a second way to empty a site, so a fast enzyme needs more substrate to keep half its sites full. Km equals Kd only when k₂ ≪ k₋₁.
cards.why: A small Km means the enzyme reaches half speed on very little substrate, whatever the reason.
cards.quote: Km equals Kd only when turnover is much slower than falling off (k₂ ≪ k₋₁), so Km is not binding affinity
cards.section: Km is the half-busy point, not the affinity

cards.front: In the minimal Michaelis–Menten scheme, an enzyme has Kd = 20 µM for its substrate and turns substrate over 4 times faster than substrate falls off (k₂ = 4 k₋₁). What is Km?
cards.back: Km = Kd + k₂/k₁ = Kd + 4(k₋₁/k₁) = 20 + 80 = 100 µM, five times Kd.
cards.quote: Split Km into two parts: Km = (k₋₁ + k₂) / k₁ = k₋₁/k₁ + k₂/k₁ = Kd + k₂/k₁
cards.section: Km is the half-busy point, not the affinity

cards.front: To get a property of the enzyme molecule rather than the tube, divide out the enzyme: kcat = {{c1::Vmax / [E]ₜ}}, in s⁻¹.
cards.back: Strictly, per active site.
cards.quote: Divide it out for a property of the molecule: kcat = Vmax / [E]ₜ, in s⁻¹ (strictly, per active site).
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: An assay with 2 nM total enzyme gives Vmax = 1.0 µM/s. What is kcat? If you repeat it with 4 nM enzyme, what happens to Vmax and kcat?
cards.back: kcat = Vmax/[E]ₜ = (1.0 × 10⁻⁶ M/s)/(2 × 10⁻⁹ M) = 500 s⁻¹. With 4 nM enzyme, Vmax doubles to 2.0 µM/s; kcat stays 500 s⁻¹.
cards.quote: Vmax depends on how much enzyme is in the tube: double the enzyme, double Vmax.
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: Why does kcat/Km, not kcat, set an enzyme's rate when substrate is scarce?
cards.back: At low [S] almost every enzyme is empty and the busy fraction is about [S]/Km, so v ≈ (kcat/Km) × [E]ₜ × [S]. kcat/Km is the rate constant for an encounter that ends in product (M⁻¹s⁻¹).
cards.quote: When substrate is scarce, almost every enzyme is empty, the busy fraction is about [S]/Km, and v ≈ (kcat/Km) × [E]ₜ × [S]
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: What sets the upper limit on kcat/Km, and about how large is it?
cards.back: The diffusion limit: how often enzyme and substrate collide in water, typically about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. Enzymes near it are called kinetically perfect.
cards.quote: It cannot exceed how often enzyme and substrate collide in water, the diffusion limit, typically about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: One enzyme can act on substrates A and B. A has the higher kcat/Km. Both are present together at equal low concentrations. Which is converted faster, and why?
cards.back: A. kcat/Km is the specificity constant, which sets an enzyme's preference among competing substrates.
cards.why: kcat/Km describes only the low-substrate regime, so it is safest for comparing substrates of one enzyme.
cards.quote: more precisely it is the specificity constant, which sets an enzyme's preference among competing substrates.
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: A metabolite in a cell sits at 3 × Km of the enzyme that uses it. What fraction of Vmax does the enzyme run at? If the metabolite doubles to 6 × Km, how much faster does the enzyme go?
cards.back: At 3 Km: 3/4 of Vmax. At 6 Km: 6/7 ≈ 0.86 of Vmax, about 14% faster. Above Km the enzyme is more than half busy but still tracks substrate changes.
cards.quote: at 3 Km an enzyme runs at three-quarters of Vmax and still tracks changes in substrate.
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v versus 1/[S]), what are the y-intercept, x-intercept and slope?
cards.back: y-intercept 1/Vmax; x-intercept −1/Km; slope Km/Vmax.
cards.why: Watch the reciprocals: the intercept is 1/Vmax, not Vmax.
cards.quote: This double-reciprocal or Lineweaver–Burk plot has y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km and slope Km/Vmax.
cards.section: Reading the curve a second way: Lineweaver–Burk

cards.front: A Lineweaver–Burk line crosses the y-axis at 0.02 min/µmol and the x-axis at −0.25 per mM. Find Vmax, Km and the slope.
cards.back: Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50 µmol/min. Km = 1/0.25 = 4 mM. Slope = Km/Vmax = 4/50 = 0.08 min·mM/µmol.
cards.quote: y-intercept: 1/Vmax = 1/100 = 0.01 min/µmol. Slope: Km/Vmax = 2/100 = 0.02. x-intercept: −1/Km = −1/2 = −0.5 per mM.
cards.section: Reading the curve a second way: Lineweaver–Burk

cards.front: Why are Km and Vmax now estimated by non-linear fitting of the hyperbola rather than from a Lineweaver–Burk plot?
cards.back: Taking reciprocals magnifies the error in the low-[S] points. The double-reciprocal plot is still used to see patterns, such as the type of inhibitor.
cards.quote: One caution: taking reciprocals magnifies the error in the low-[S] points.
cards.section: Reading the curve a second way: Lineweaver–Burk

cards.front: Why does a competitive inhibitor raise the apparent Km but leave Vmax unchanged?
cards.back: It ties up free enzyme, so more substrate is needed to make half the enzyme busy (Km rises). At very high [S] almost no free enzyme is left for it, so Vmax is unchanged.
cards.quote: But flood the system with substrate and almost no free enzyme is left for the inhibitor, so Vmax is unchanged and the Lineweaver–Burk lines share a y-intercept.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: A competitive inhibitor is present at [I] = Ki, so its factor 1 + [I]/Ki = 2. What fraction of Vmax is reached at [S] = Km, and what share of the uninhibited velocity is lost?
cards.back: Apparent Km = 2 Km. v = Vmax × Km/(2 Km + Km) = ⅓ Vmax, versus ½ Vmax without inhibitor: one third of the velocity lost.
cards.quote: For worked numbers, take an inhibitor dose that makes its factor, 1 + [I]/Ki, equal to 3 (that is, [I] = 2 Ki).
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: Why does an uncompetitive inhibitor lower both apparent Vmax and apparent Km, and what does its Lineweaver–Burk plot look like?
cards.back: It binds only ES, forming ESI. Pulling ES away draws more E + S into ES (Le Chatelier), lowering apparent Km, while the stuck ESI lowers Vmax. Both fall by the same factor: parallel lines.
cards.quote: Both fall by the same factor, leaving the slope, Km/Vmax, unchanged: parallel lines.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: A drug is an uncompetitive inhibitor of an enzyme in a pathway. As the enzyme slows, its substrate builds up. Does the build-up relieve the inhibition or worsen it? Why?
cards.back: It worsens it. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only ES, and more substrate makes more ES for it to grab, so the share of velocity lost grows as [S] rises.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the inhibitor's pattern is set by which enzyme pool it ties up (here ES only).
cards.quote: More, because more substrate makes more ES for it to grab.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: Why does a pure noncompetitive inhibitor lower Vmax but leave Km unchanged?
cards.back: It binds away from the active site, equally well to E and ES. Taking the same share out of both is like having less enzyme: Vmax falls, Km unchanged, lines share the x-intercept (−1/Km).
cards.quote: Taking the same share out of E and ES is like having less enzyme: Vmax falls, Km unchanged, so the lines share the x-intercept (−1/Km).
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: Lineweaver–Burk lines with and without a reversible inhibitor meet on the x-axis; the inhibited line has a higher y-intercept. What kind of inhibitor is it, and what does it bind?
cards.back: Pure noncompetitive. Same −1/Km means Km is unchanged; higher 1/Vmax means Vmax fell. It binds a site away from the active site, to E and ES equally well.
cards.quote: The inhibitor binds a site away from the active site, equally well with or without substrate.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: An irreversible inactivator is added to an enzyme and allowed to finish reacting. What Lineweaver–Burk pattern results, compared with the untreated enzyme, and why?
cards.back: The pure noncompetitive pattern: Vmax falls, Km unchanged, lines share the x-intercept. The inactivator simply leaves less working enzyme.
cards.quote: An irreversible inactivator that has finished reacting gives the same plot, because it simply leaves less enzyme.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: An inhibitor at fixed concentration cuts V₀ in half at [S] = Km. Design a simple test of whether it is competitive or pure noncompetitive, and state the expected results.
cards.back: Measure V₀ with and without inhibitor at very high [S] (say 100 Km). Competitive: the share of v lost shrinks toward zero (about 2% at 100 Km). Noncompetitive: the share lost stays the same.
cards.why: Rests on which pool each ties up: competitive binds only free E, which high [S] removes; noncompetitive takes the same share of E and ES.
cards.quote: The same arithmetic gives about 15% lost at 10 Km and only about 2% at 100 Km.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: Why are stable transition-state analogs among the most potent reversible enzyme inhibitors?
cards.back: The active site is shaped to grip the fleeting transition state more tightly than the substrate, so a stable mimic of that state binds the active site very tightly.
cards.quote: stable mimics of that state, transition-state analogs, make some of the most potent inhibitors known.
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors

cards.front: Enzyme concentration in an assay is comparable to Km. Someone reads Km as the added [S] that gives half of Vmax. Is the half-busy point reached at an added [S] = Km? Why?
cards.back: No. Much of the substrate sits on the enzyme, so free [S] is below the added [S]; at an added [S] = Km the busy fraction falls below one half (about 0.38 when [E]ₜ = Km).
cards.why: Rests on the model's assumption that free [S] is about the [S] added, which needs far more substrate than enzyme.
cards.quote: With enzyme concentration comparable to Km, much of the substrate sits on the enzyme, and the busy fraction at an added [S] = Km falls below one half
cards.section: Where the model stops

cards.front: What v versus [S] curve shape do cooperative enzymes give, and what is reported instead of Km?
cards.back: Sigmoidal curves (usually allosteric, multi-subunit enzymes). K₀.₅ is reported rather than a mechanistic Km.
cards.quote: Cooperative enzymes, usually allosteric multi-subunit ones, give sigmoidal v–[S] curves
cards.section: Where the model stops

cards.front: An enzyme forms an acyl-enzyme intermediate that breaks down slowly. Can its Km be smaller than its Kd for substrate? Why?
cards.back: Yes. With a slow step after ES, enzyme piles up in that busy form, so Km can fall below Kd. Km = Kd + k₂/k₁ holds only for the minimal scheme. Km is still the [S] at half of Vmax.
cards.quote: With a slow step after ES, such as an acyl-enzyme intermediate, enzyme piles up in that busy form, so Km can be smaller than Kd.
cards.section: When Km is below Kd

cards.front: Where does an enzyme's catalytic power come from, in terms of the transition state?
cards.back: From gripping the transition state more tightly than the substrate: the binding energy released pays down the activation barrier, ΔG‡.
cards.quote: That tighter grip on the transition state is where catalysis comes from: the binding energy released pays down ΔG‡ (Pauling's insight).
cards.section: From lock and key to the transition state

cards.front: A substrate analog binds an enzyme's active site well, but its transition state fits the site poorly. Predict its kcat/Km relative to the natural substrate, and explain.
cards.back: Lower: it is turned over slowly even though it binds. kcat/Km reflects how tightly the enzyme binds each substrate's transition state, not the substrate itself.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that transition-state binding energy underlies both catalysis and specificity.
cards.quote: so a substrate whose transition state fits the site poorly is turned over slowly even if it binds.
cards.section: From lock and key to the transition state

cards.front: For one enzyme, Lineweaver–Burk lines for substrates X and Y share a y-intercept. X crosses the x-axis at −0.5 per mM, Y at −0.05 per mM. Find each Km, compare kcat, and say which is preferred when both compete at low concentration.
cards.back: Km(X) = 2 mM, Km(Y) = 20 mM. Same y-intercept means same Vmax, so same kcat. kcat/Km is 10 times higher for X, so X is preferred.
cards.why: Combines x-intercept = −1/Km and y-intercept = 1/Vmax with kcat/Km as the specificity constant for substrates of one enzyme.
cards.quote: It is safest for comparing substrates of one enzyme: ranking different enzymes by it can mislead, because it describes only the low-substrate regime.
cards.section: Speed and efficiency: kcat and kcat/Km

cards.front: At very low [S] (far below Km), a competitive inhibitor is added at [I] = 2 Ki. By what factor does the velocity fall?
cards.back: Threefold. The factor 1 + [I]/Ki = 3 raises apparent Km to 3 Km. At low [S], v ≈ (kcat/Km_app) × [E]ₜ × [S], so v drops to one third.
cards.why: Combines the low-substrate rate law with the competitive rule that only apparent Km changes.
cards.quote: It takes more substrate to make half the enzyme busy, so the apparent Km rises (here, threefold).
cards.section: When something gets in the way: inhibitors
